title: Read and repair try/catch tests
summary: Trace both outcomes of an exception test, then preserve useful information when an exception crosses a boundary.
goals: Explain why a manual exception test needs a no-exception failure path.
Trace which catch runs and whether execution continues or propagates.
Rethrow with context while preserving the original cause.
setup: You can already use assertThrows. Now read the older manual form: the call runs inside try, and a matching catch handles the exception. A test must check what happens if the expected exception is missing as well as when it appears.

worked.title: A complete manual exception test
worked.intro:
This self-contained example puts the small production helper and its test in the same class so every name is visible. The helper is the code under test; the test returns void.

import org.junit.jupiter.api.Test;
import static org.junit.jupiter.api.Assertions.*;

class PositiveAmountTest {
    static void requirePositive(int amount) {
        if (amount <= 0) {
            throw new IllegalArgumentException("amount must be positive");
        }
    }

    @Test
    void zeroAmount_isRejected() {
        try {
            requirePositive(0);
            fail("Expected an IllegalArgumentException for zero");
        } catch (IllegalArgumentException ex) {
            assertEquals("amount must be positive", ex.getMessage());
        }
    }
}

steps.title: Follow the correct implementation
steps.html: requirePositive(0) throws. Control skips fail and enters the matching catch. The assertion checks the promised message.

steps.title: Follow a broken implementation
steps.html: Suppose the helper returns normally for zero. Execution reaches fail, so the test fails. Without that line, the test would finish successfully without checking anything.

steps.title: Follow an unexpected exception
steps.html: If the helper throws NullPointerException, the narrow catch does not handle it. The test ends with that unexpected exception; it does not silently pass.

steps.title: Read the shorter equivalent
steps.html:
IllegalArgumentException ex = assertThrows(
    IllegalArgumentException.class, () -> requirePositive(0));
assertEquals("amount must be positive", ex.getMessage());

Both forms reject normal completion and check the message. The lambda keeps the action inside the assertion.

sections.title: Handling, propagating and translating are different decisions
sections.html:
Handling means the current method has a defined response and can continue. Propagating means letting a caller decide. Translating means throwing a different exception that describes the higher-level operation. When translating, keep the cause instead of discarding the original evidence.

The new call here is Integer.parseInt(text): it converts decimal text such as "12" into the int 12 and throws NumberFormatException for text such as "twelve". We use that existing failure to practise adding context.

static int readCount(String text) {
    try {
        return Integer.parseInt(text);
    } catch (NumberFormatException ex) {
        throw new IllegalArgumentException("Count must be an integer", ex);
    }
}

The two constructor arguments are the new message and the original exception. ex becomes the cause of the new exception; getCause() returns that original object. A caller can inspect getCause(), and a stack trace can show both layers. A throws declaration documents or declares propagation; it does not itself throw anything.

sections.title: Avoid catches that make a test meaningless
sections.html: A catch that merely prints an exception can turn a failed operation into a passing test. Catch the expected type and assert the promised information. Do not catch Throwable around assertions: it can also catch assertion failures. A plain catch (Exception ex) is already too broad for a test intended to expect one particular runtime exception.

practice.title: What does the missing fail allow?
practice.prompt:
// Contract: amount must be positive. Nonpositive amounts throw
// IllegalArgumentException with message "amount must be positive".
static void requirePositive(int amount) {
    if (amount <= 0) {
        throw new IllegalArgumentException("amount must be positive");
    }
}
@Test
void rejectsZero() {
    try { requirePositive(0); }
    catch (IllegalArgumentException ex) { /* expected */ }
}

If a faulty implementation accepts zero and returns normally, what happens?
practice.hint: Trace the path when no exception is thrown.
practice.solution: It passes. Add fail(...) after the call, or use assertThrows.

options.text: The test passes without detecting the defect.
options.feedback: The try completes, the catch is skipped, and no assertion fails.

options.text: The test fails because a catch was skipped.
options.feedback: Skipping a catch is normal when no exception is thrown.

options.text: The test does not compile because try needs fail.
options.feedback: Java permits this structure; the defect is in the test’s reasoning.

practice.title: Preserve the cause
practice.prompt:
This snippet is the body of static int readCount(String text). Integer.parseInt converts valid decimal text to int and throws NumberFormatException for invalid numeric text.

try {
    return Integer.parseInt(text);
} catch (NumberFormatException ex) {
    throw new IllegalArgumentException("Invalid count", ex);
}

Which statements are correct?
practice.hint: Distinguish the exception object from the result the method normally returns.
practice.solution: The first two statements are correct. Translation adds context while preserving the lower-level exception.

options.text: The thrown exception has the message "Invalid count".
options.feedback: That is the message passed to the new exception.

options.text: The original NumberFormatException is available through getCause().
options.feedback: The two-argument constructor records ex as the cause.

options.text: The caller receives a normal integer result after the catch.
options.feedback: The catch throws, so the method does not return normally on this path.

options.text: The catch retries parseInt automatically.
options.feedback: A catch runs its body; no retry occurs unless explicitly programmed.

practice.title: Repair a manual test
practice.prompt:
// Contract: amount must be positive. Nonpositive amounts throw
// IllegalArgumentException with message "amount must be positive".
static void requirePositive(int amount) {
    if (amount <= 0) {
        throw new IllegalArgumentException("amount must be positive");
    }
}
@Test
void rejectsNegative() {
    try {
        requirePositive(-2);
    } catch (Exception ex) {
        System.out.println(ex.getMessage());
    }
}

Rewrite this as a reliable manual try/catch test. Assume Jupiter imports are present.
practice.hint: Reject normal completion, catch the promised type, and check the documented message.
practice.solution:
@Test
void rejectsNegative() {
    try {
        requirePositive(-2);
        fail("Expected a rejection for -2");
    } catch (IllegalArgumentException ex) {
        assertEquals("amount must be positive", ex.getMessage());
    }
}
rubric: The test is a void @Test method with a well-typed call.
fail occurs immediately after the action in the try block.
The catch expects IllegalArgumentException rather than every Exception.
The expected message is the first assertEquals argument.

practice.title: Explain all three paths
practice.prompt:
Assume load() can return normally, throw IllegalArgumentException, or throw IllegalStateException. No other code throws.

String trace = "A";
try {
    load();
    trace += "B";
} catch (IllegalArgumentException ex) {
    trace += "C";
} finally {
    trace += "D";
}
trace += "E";

Give the final trace for normal return and the handled exception. For the unhandled exception, give the trace just before it leaves this code and say whether E is appended.
practice.hint: finally runs during both normal completion and propagation here.
practice.solution:
OutcomeTraceReason
Normal returnABDEThe try finishes, then finally and the following statement run.
IllegalArgumentExceptionACDEB is skipped; catch, finally and E run.
IllegalStateExceptionAD before propagationNo matching catch; finally runs, then the exception leaves. E is skipped.
rubric: Normal result is ABDE.
Handled result is ACDE.
Unhandled path runs finally, has AD, and does not reach E.

teachBack.prompt: Why does a manual exception test need to reason about the path where no exception happens?
teachBack.answer: That is exactly the path a missing validation bug produces. A test must fail on that path; otherwise the absence of the required exception becomes a false pass.

bridge: Next, place validation in production code and distinguish it from assertions used inside tests.

title: Validate before you depend on an input
summary: Turn a contract into ordered guards, and distinguish Java assert from JUnit assertions.
goals: Order guards so invalid inputs are rejected before dereferencing or mutation.
Write separate tests for independent invalid conditions and preserved state.
Explain when Java assert can disappear and why JUnit assertions differ.
setup: An input can have the right Java type and still violate a method’s rules. Defensive code checks the documented conditions before using the input. An invariant is a condition the object must preserve; a guard is ordinary code that rejects a specific invalid call.

worked.title: A safe array update and its tests
worked.intro:
import org.junit.jupiter.api.Test;
import static org.junit.jupiter.api.Assertions.*;

class ArrayUpdateTest {
    // Throws NPE for null values, then IndexOutOfBoundsException
    // for index outside [0, values.length). Invalid calls change nothing.
    static void replace(int[] values, int index, int replacement) {
        if (values == null) {
            throw new NullPointerException("values must not be null");
        }
        if (index < 0 || index >= values.length) {
            throw new IndexOutOfBoundsException("invalid index");
        }
        values[index] = replacement;
    }

    @Test
    void indexAtLength_isRejected_withoutChangingArray() {
        int[] values = new int[]{4, 9};
        assertThrows(IndexOutOfBoundsException.class,
            () -> replace(values, 2, 7));
        assertArrayEquals(new int[]{4, 9}, values);
    }
}

steps.title: Read the type separately from the range
steps.html: 2 is an int, so the call compiles. Its value is invalid for this two-element array, whose legal indexes are 0 and 1.

steps.title: Check null before reading length
steps.html: values.length needs a real array. The null guard comes first, which also implements the stated precedence when both arguments are invalid.

steps.title: Check both ends before writing
steps.html: The second guard rejects negatives and indexes at or beyond the length. Only a valid index reaches the assignment.

steps.title: Observe the whole promise
steps.html: The test checks the exception and the unchanged array. Both observations belong to one scenario: rejecting this update without modifying state. A test can contain more than one assertion when they check related effects.

sections.title: Three different meanings of “assert”
sections.html:
FormWhere it belongsWhat to remember
assert condition;Java language statement for internal assumptionsWith -ea, a false condition throws AssertionError. When disabled, the check is skipped. Do not use it for required public argument validation.
assertEquals(expected, actual)JUnit testRuns as a normal library call; does not depend on -ea.
if (bad) throw ...;Production validationRuns normally whether Java assertions are enabled or disabled.

Calling an input check “defensive” does not choose its exception class. The method’s contract determines whether the response is an exception, a return value, or another documented result.

sections.title: Isolate conditions, then consider interactions
sections.html: For an index guard, use a valid non-null array while testing the lower and upper limits. Test null separately. If the contract gives precedence for multiple invalid arguments, add an interaction case. If it says nothing about precedence, do not invent an exact exception choice for a call violating several conditions.

practice.title: Which check must happen first?
practice.prompt: Contract: size(String text) throws IllegalArgumentException with message "missing text" for null; otherwise returns its length. Which implementation meets it?
practice.hint: Which operation first needs an actual String object?
practice.solution: Check for null first with ordinary control flow, then call length().

options.text: if (text == null) throw new IllegalArgumentException("missing text"); return text.length();
options.feedback: The null check uses no dereference and throws the documented type before reading length.

options.text: int n = text.length(); if (text == null) throw new IllegalArgumentException("missing text"); return n;
options.feedback: Null fails at text.length() with NullPointerException before the intended guard.

options.text: assert text != null; return text.length();
options.feedback: A disabled assertion does not validate input, and an enabled one throws AssertionError rather than the promised type.

practice.title: Select independent boundary tests
practice.prompt: For a three-element array, replace(int[] a, int index, int value) requires 0 ≤ index < 3. Which cases separately check both nearest invalid boundaries while keeping the array valid?
practice.hint: The final valid index is one less than the length.
practice.solution: Use -1 and 3 with a non-null three-element array. Also test valid indexes 0 and 2 in the normal-behavior suite.

options.text: replace(new int[]{2, 4, 6}, -1, 8)
options.feedback: -1 is the nearest value below the legal range.

options.text: replace(new int[]{2, 4, 6}, 3, 8)
options.feedback: 3 equals the length and is the nearest value above the valid indexes.

options.text: replace(null, -1, 8)
options.feedback: This violates both nullability and the index rule; it does not isolate the index guard.

options.text: replace(new int[]{2, 4, 6}, 2, 8)
options.feedback: This is an important valid upper-boundary test, but it is not an invalid boundary.

practice.title: Replace a disappearing guard
practice.prompt:
Contract: setLimit(int n) accepts zero or positive values; negative values throw IllegalArgumentException and leave the old limit unchanged. The class starts with private int limit = 5; and has int getLimit().

void setLimit(int n) {
    assert n >= 0;
    limit = n;
}

Repair the method, then write a Jupiter test for the rejected update. The class is named Limit and has a no-argument constructor.

Assume org.junit.jupiter.api.Test and the static org.junit.jupiter.api.Assertions.* imports are present. Write the test methods inside a test class in the same package as the supplied API.
practice.hint: Use an if guard before assignment; observe both the exception and state.
practice.solution:
void setLimit(int n) {
    if (n < 0) {
        throw new IllegalArgumentException("limit must be nonnegative");
    }
    limit = n;
}

@Test
void negativeLimit_preservesPreviousValue() {
    Limit limit = new Limit();
    assertThrows(IllegalArgumentException.class, () -> limit.setLimit(-1));
    assertEquals(5, limit.getLimit());
}
rubric: Ordinary if/throw enforces the contract without -ea.
The assignment happens only after validation.
The test uses -1, checks the specified exception and observes the old value 5.
No exception-message requirement is invented.

practice.title: Find the guard that cannot protect anything
practice.prompt:
// Contract: reject null with IllegalArgumentException.
// Otherwise return true for an empty String and false for a nonempty String.
static boolean isEmpty(String value) {
    if (value.length() == 0 || value == null) {
        return true;
    }
    return false;
}

Give a revealing input, the expected and actual behavior, and a corrected implementation.
practice.hint: Short-circuit evaluation goes from left to right. Also read the specified null response.
practice.solution:
Input null should throw IllegalArgumentException. It actually throws NullPointerException while evaluating value.length(). Simply swapping the operands still returns true for null, which contradicts the contract.

static boolean isEmpty(String value) {
    if (value == null) {
        throw new IllegalArgumentException("value must not be null");
    }
    return value.length() == 0;
}
rubric: Identifies the dereference before the null test.
States the correct expected exception from the contract.
Does not “repair” the code by returning true for null.

teachBack.prompt: Why can a JUnit test still fail when Java assertions are disabled?
teachBack.answer: JUnit assertion methods are ordinary method calls that report test failures. They are different from the optional Java assert statement.

bridge: Next, use concrete inputs to explain production defects precisely.

title: Explain a bug with a revealing input
summary: Connect the contract, one execution trace and the faulty operation instead of naming a suspicious line alone.
goals: Distinguish compile-time, unexpected-exception and logical defects.
Choose a small input that reaches and exposes the faulty operation.
Explain a repair in terms of required behavior.
setup: A suspicious expression is the start of an investigation. A convincing explanation gives a witness: a concrete input that makes required and actual behavior differ. First decide whether the code compiles. A method that cannot compile has no runtime trace to test.

worked.title: The return that ends the search too soon
worked.intro:
// Return the first index containing target, or -1 if absent.
// values must be non-null.
static int find(int[] values, int target) {
    for (int i = 0; i < values.length; i++) {
        if (values[i] == target) {
            return i;
        }
        return -1; // suspect line
    }
    return -1;
}

Witness: values = {4, 9} and target = 9. Expected index: 1. Actual return: -1.

steps.title: Read the promise
steps.html: The method must search for the first occurrence anywhere in the array. “Absent” means no element matches, not merely that the first element differs.

steps.title: Trace the witness
steps.html: At i = 0, the comparison 4 == 9 is false. The inner return -1 immediately exits the method. The loop never reaches index 1.

steps.title: Classify the defect
steps.html: The code compiles and does not throw for this input. It returns a wrong value, so this is a logical defect. The test assertEquals(1, find(new int[]{4, 9}, 9)) fails.

steps.title: Repair the cause
steps.html: Remove the inner return -1. The return after the loop handles absence only after every candidate has been examined. Keep successful early return inside the matching branch.

sections.title: Common patterns require different witnesses
sections.html:
PatternUseful witnessWhy it helps
i <= a.lengthAn empty array, or an absent targetExecution reaches the illegal index equal to length. An early successful return might hide it.
Replacement uses old + newStart with a nonzero old valueStarting from zero makes addition look like replacement.
x > bound instead of x >= boundUse x exactly equal to boundOrdinary values on either side do not distinguish these operators.
Integer division where a fraction is promisedUse 5 divided by 2With two int operands, 5 / 2 produces 2: Java discards the fractional part. If the contract promises 2.5, a double operand such as 5.0 / 2 changes the calculation. Evenly divisible inputs hide this difference.
Missing loop progressAn input that enters the repeating pathExplain which state should move toward termination but does not.

A witness must satisfy documented preconditions unless invalid-input handling is the subject. Otherwise the contract may provide no expected behavior.

sections.title: Separate illegal Java from incorrect behavior
sections.html:
static int count() { return null; } // does not compile
static int first(int[] a) { return a[0]; } // compiles; needs a contract
static int doubleValue(int x) { return x + 1; } // compiles; likely wrong contract

The first returns a reference value where an int is required. Whether the second is defective depends on its preconditions and promised handling of empty arrays. For the third, compare its behavior to the actual promise; the name alone is not a complete specification.

practice.title: Choose the witness that reaches the defect
practice.prompt:
// Return the first index containing target, or -1 if absent.
// values must be non-null.
static int find(int[] values, int target) {
    for (int i = 0; i < values.length; i++) {
        if (values[i] == target) {
            return i;
        }
        return -1; // suspect line
    }
    return -1;
}

Which test exposes the premature return?
practice.hint: Make the first comparison false but a later comparison true.
practice.solution: The second-position match is the revealing case. First-position and absent cases remain useful regression cases, but they do not expose this bug.

options.text: assertEquals(1, find(new int[]{4, 9}, 9));
options.feedback: The target is after a nonmatching first element, so the premature return hides it.

options.text: assertEquals(0, find(new int[]{9, 4}, 9));
options.feedback: The first element matches and returns correctly before the defect matters.

options.text: assertEquals(-1, find(new int[]{4}, 9));
options.feedback: The returned -1 happens to be correct for an absent target.

practice.title: Classify the evidence
practice.prompt: Select the statements that correctly describe the shown Java.
practice.hint: Ask separately whether the statement is legal Java and what execution would do.
practice.solution: The first two classifications are correct. A logical defect need not throw, and passing without observations provides no behavioral evidence.

options.text: int result = "4"; is a compile-time type error.
options.feedback: A String cannot be assigned directly to an int.

options.text: For int[] a = new int[]{3}, evaluating a[1] produces an out-of-bounds exception.
options.feedback: The array has one element, at index 0.

options.text: Returning 7 when the contract requires 8 must produce an exception.
options.feedback: A wrong result can return normally; an assertion can detect it.

options.text: An empty test method proves the production method is correct.
options.feedback: An empty body may pass without calling or checking the production code.

practice.title: Repair a boundary condition
practice.prompt:
// Returns the number of positive elements in a non-null array.
static int positives(int[] values) {
    int count = 0;
    for (int i = 0; i <= values.length; i++) {
        if (values[i] > 0) count++;
    }
    return count;
}

Give the smallest allowed revealing input. Explain expected versus actual behavior, identify the repair, and write one regression assertion.
practice.hint: An empty array is non-null and requires zero loop iterations.
practice.solution:
Use new int[0]. The expected count is 0. The loop enters with i = 0 because 0 <= 0, then attempts index 0 and throws. Change the guard to i < values.length.

assertEquals(0, positives(new int[0]));
rubric: Uses a non-null input that satisfies the contract.
Explains the exact out-of-bounds access.
Changes <= to < and states why.
Expected count appears first in the assertion.

practice.title: Explain a replacement bug
practice.prompt:
A Score starts at 3. void set(int value) must replace the score with value; int get() returns it. The implementation is:

void set(int value) {
    score += value;
}

Write a full Jupiter test method using new Score(), then explain why starting at zero would be a weaker witness.

Assume org.junit.jupiter.api.Test and the static org.junit.jupiter.api.Assertions.* imports are present. Write the test methods inside a test class in the same package as the supplied API.
practice.hint: Use different nonzero old and new values.
practice.solution:
@Test
void set_replacesExistingScore() {
    Score score = new Score();
    score.set(5);
    assertEquals(5, score.get());
}

The faulty implementation returns 8. If the old score were zero, adding 5 would also yield 5, so that setup would not distinguish replacement from accumulation.
rubric: Creates the stated fixture and calls set with an int.
Asserts replacement value 5 rather than accumulated 8.
Connects the nonzero initial state to the fault’s visibility.

teachBack.prompt: What makes “the return is in the wrong place” an incomplete bug explanation?
teachBack.answer: It gives neither a required behavior nor evidence of a violation. Add a specific input, trace where execution ends, and show the expected result that was missed.

bridge: Next, inspect defects that appear across several operations because an object’s representation becomes inconsistent.

title: Keep the representation consistent
summary: Use ADT behavior and representation invariants to uncover state defects, copying errors and cascades.
goals: Explain an invariant as a relationship that every public operation preserves.
Test empty, singleton and multi-element transitions through public operations.
Distinguish independent copies from aliases and design a mutation witness.
setup: An ADT describes allowed operations and behavior. Its implementation chooses a representation, such as linked nodes plus a stored count. A representation invariant connects those pieces. If size claims there are two nodes while the chain contains one, several public methods can become wrong at once.

worked.title: One missing update, several symptoms
worked.intro:
IntQueue is a first-in, first-out queue. A new queue is empty. void add(int) appends; int remove() returns and removes the oldest value, throwing NoSuchElementException when empty. int size() counts stored values, and boolean isEmpty() is true exactly when no values remain.

A node is a small object holding an int value and a reference next to the following node. head refers to the first node; tail to the last. The last node has next == null. Following next references from head visits the reachable nodes. The separate int field size should count them. In a one-node queue, head and tail refer to that same node.

// Inside IntQueue; head/tail reference linked nodes and size counts them.
int remove() {
    if (head == null) throw new java.util.NoSuchElementException();
    int result = head.value;
    head = head.next;
    if (head == null) tail = null;
    return result; // size was never decreased
}
@Test
void removeOnlyElement_leavesEmptyQueue() {
    IntQueue queue = new IntQueue();
    queue.add(7);
    assertEquals(7, queue.remove());
    assertEquals(0, queue.size());
    assertTrue(queue.isEmpty());
}

Assume size() returns the stored size and isEmpty() evaluates size == 0. Jupiter imports are present.

steps.title: State the invariant
steps.html: size must equal the number of reachable nodes. An empty queue has head == null, tail == null and size == 0. For a nonempty queue, tail identifies the last reachable node.

steps.title: Trace the singleton removal
steps.html: After adding 7, size is 1 and both ends refer to that node. Removing it makes head and tail null. The missing decrement leaves size equal to 1.

steps.title: Connect symptoms to one cause
steps.html: The returned value is correct. The size assertion fails; isEmpty() would also be false if checked separately. These observations point to one omitted state update, not automatically two independent defects.

steps.title: Repair and check another transition
steps.html: Add size--; after removing a node. Also test a two-element queue: removing the first element must leave size 1 and the second value available. After emptying, add again to check that the end pointers still work.

sections.title: Which invariants matter depends on the representation
sections.html:
RepresentationPossible invariantRevealing operation
Linked queueCount equals reachable nodes; tail is lastRemove only element, then add again.
Sorted collectionEvery adjacent key is in orderInsert before first, between two, and after last.
Sparse countsAbsent means zero; stored entries are nonzeroSet an existing count to zero, and set zero for an absent key.
Independent copyMutable representation is not sharedMutate the copy and inspect the original.

Do not assume every ADT uses these rules. They are stated design choices. White-box reasoning uses the actual representation; black-box tests still observe the public promises.

sections.title: Equal contents do not prove an independent copy
sections.html:
int[] original = new int[]{2, 5};
int[] alias = original;
int[] copy = original.clone();
alias[0] = 9; // original[0] also becomes 9
copy[1] = 8;  // original[1] remains 5

A reference assignment copies the reference, so alias and original name the same array. An array clone makes a new array. For arrays containing mutable objects, cloning the array alone still shares its element objects; a deeper independence promise needs additional copying. Choose tests based on the documented depth of copying.

A collection wrapper is an object holding a reference to its storage array. Constructing a different wrapper does not automatically copy that array. This is why the later IntStore task changes a value in the copy and then observes the original.

practice.title: Find the inconsistent state
practice.prompt:
IntQueue is a first-in, first-out queue. A new queue is empty. void add(int) appends; int remove() returns and removes the oldest value, throwing NoSuchElementException when empty. int size() counts stored values, and boolean isEmpty() is true exactly when no values remain.

A node is a small object holding an int value and a reference next to the following node. head refers to the first node; tail to the last. The last node has next == null. Following next references from head visits the reachable nodes. The separate int field size should count them. In a one-node queue, head and tail refer to that same node.

// Inside IntQueue; head/tail reference linked nodes and size counts them.
int remove() {
    if (head == null) throw new java.util.NoSuchElementException();
    int result = head.value;
    head = head.next;
    if (head == null) tail = null;
    return result; // size was never decreased
}

Start with one node containing 7 and size 1. After remove returns, which state does the shown code leave?
practice.hint: Track each field independently; do not assume the invariant maintains itself.
practice.solution: The pointer representation is empty while the stored count remains 1.

options.text: head = null, tail = null, size = 1
options.feedback: The pointers change, but size is never decremented.

options.text: head = null, tail = null, size = 0
options.feedback: That is the desired state; the missing update prevents it.

options.text: head still points to 7 and size = 1
options.feedback: head is explicitly moved to head.next, which is null for the only node.

practice.title: Choose evidence for copy independence
practice.prompt: IntStore copy() promises an independent copy of an integer collection. get(int) reads and set(int,int) replaces a value. Which observations directly check parts of that promise?
practice.hint: Equality now and independence after mutation answer different questions.
practice.solution: Check initial values and a later mutation. Identity checks alone cannot establish whether internal mutable storage is shared.

options.text: The copy initially contains the same integer values.
options.feedback: A copy must preserve the original values initially.

options.text: Changing a value in the copy leaves the original value unchanged.
options.feedback: This reveals shared mutable storage if the promise is violated.

options.text: The copy has the same toString output before either object is changed, so no other checks are needed.
options.feedback: Equal initial output does not establish independent storage.

options.text: assertSame(original, copy) proves independence.
options.feedback: assertSame requires the same object, which contradicts a distinct independent copy.

practice.title: Test a state sequence
practice.prompt:
IntQueue is a first-in, first-out queue. A new queue is empty. void add(int) appends; int remove() returns and removes the oldest value, throwing NoSuchElementException when empty. int size() counts stored values, and boolean isEmpty() is true exactly when no values remain.

Write a Jupiter test that adds 4 then 9, removes 4, checks size 1, removes 9, checks emptiness, adds 6, then removes 6. Explain what the final add/remove can reveal.

Assume org.junit.jupiter.api.Test and the static org.junit.jupiter.api.Assertions.* imports are present. Write the test methods inside a test class in the same package as the supplied API.
practice.hint: Each operation changes the state used by the next observation.
practice.solution:
@Test
void queue_reusesStorageAfterBecomingEmpty() {
    IntQueue queue = new IntQueue();
    queue.add(4);
    queue.add(9);
    assertEquals(4, queue.remove());
    assertEquals(1, queue.size());
    assertEquals(9, queue.remove());
    assertTrue(queue.isEmpty());
    queue.add(6);
    assertEquals(6, queue.remove());
    assertEquals(0, queue.size());
}

Reusing the emptied queue can expose a stale tail or a broken empty-to-nonempty transition. The sequence also checks FIFO order and count updates.
rubric: Uses a fresh queue and observes the stated order.
Checks the intermediate size after only one removal.
Reuses the empty queue and checks the final state.
Explains an invariant or transition rather than merely saying “edge case.”

practice.title: Expose an aliasing copy
practice.prompt:
new IntStore(new int[]{2,5}) creates a collection with those values. Its copy() promises a separate collection whose changes cannot affect the original. set(index,value) and get(index) use zero-based indexes. A faulty copy() returns a new wrapper sharing the same internal array. Write a test that catches this, even though assertNotSame(original, copy) passes.

Assume org.junit.jupiter.api.Test and the static org.junit.jupiter.api.Assertions.* imports are present. Write the test methods inside a test class in the same package as the supplied API.
practice.hint: Change the copied collection and read the original through its public API.
practice.solution:
@Test
void copyMutation_doesNotChangeOriginal() {
    IntStore original = new IntStore(new int[]{2, 5});
    IntStore copy = original.copy();
    copy.set(0, 9);
    assertEquals(9, copy.get(0));
    assertEquals(2, original.get(0));
}

A new wrapper is not enough: shared internal storage still makes the original report 9. The second assertion observes the violated promise.
rubric: Creates distinct initial and replacement values.
Mutates only the copy.
Observes the original’s unchanged value, not merely wrapper identity.

teachBack.prompt: Why can several failing tests describe one underlying bug?
teachBack.answer: Several operations may depend on one invariant or shared helper. A missing count update can make size, emptiness and iteration disagree. Trace the common state before treating each symptom as a separate cause.

bridge: Next, apply the same scrutiny to the tests themselves.

title: Debug the test before blaming the method
summary: Identify false passes, wrong expected values, invalid fixtures and assertions that ask the wrong question.
goals: Separate an invalid test from a production failure.
Repair missing or weak assertions using an independent expected result.
Spot shared state, aliasing and exception-source mistakes.
setup: A test is code and can contain defects. A red result can mean the production code violates its contract, but it can also mean the test calls the API incorrectly or expects the wrong result. A green result can be weak evidence when the test never checks the promised behavior.

worked.title: A test that agrees with every returned answer
worked.intro:
Contract: static int capAtTen(int n) returns n when n ≤ 10 and returns 10 otherwise. Negative integers are allowed. Assume the method is available in the test class and Jupiter imports are present.

@Test
void largeInput_isCapped() {
    int result = capAtTen(14);
    assertEquals(result, result);
}

Corrected test:

@Test
void largeInput_isCapped() {
    int result = capAtTen(14);
    assertEquals(10, result, "Inputs above 10 must be capped at 10");
}

steps.title: Read what the original actually compares
steps.html: Both assertion arguments are the same local variable. Whether the method returns 10, 14 or -200, this equality succeeds. The test could still end with an unexpected exception, but it cannot detect a wrong integer result.

steps.title: Derive the oracle independently
steps.html: The contract says any input above 10 returns 10. Compute that expectation from the rule before examining the implementation’s answer.

steps.title: Check types and roles
steps.html: 14 is an allowed int argument; result is an int return value. assertEquals(10, result) checks the value. assertTrue(result) does not compile because an int is not a boolean.

steps.title: Check whether this is a useful case
steps.html: Input 14 distinguishes capping from returning every input unchanged. Add 10 for the boundary and a value below 10 for the other behavior. A correct assertion still needs a useful input.

sections.title: Audit a test in a fixed order
sections.html:
• Fixture: is the receiver real, and is the starting state the one the test needs?
  • Call: do argument types, order and count match the signature?
  • Expected result: does it follow the current contract, independently of the implementation?
  • Observation: does the assertion inspect the relevant return value, exception or state?
  • Isolation: could another test or an earlier setup failure determine this result?

Reversing assertEquals(expected, actual) often still compares the same values and compiles, but it mislabels a failure report. That is different from using the wrong expected value or an assertion with the wrong parameter type.

sections.title: Common false-positive patterns
sections.html:
These are separate test fragments, not one method. The first two use observed int values; the array fragment uses an int[] actual. In the last fragment, assume Service(int) rejects a negative constructor argument and run() is the intended operation.

assertEquals(actual, actual);              // compares a value to itself
assertTrue(result >= 0);                   // too weak if exact value is promised
int[] expected = actual;                  // aliases the produced array
assertArrayEquals(expected, actual);       // same array on both sides

assertThrows(IllegalArgumentException.class, () -> {
    Service service = new Service(-1);     // setup itself might throw
    service.run();                        // intended action may never run
});

Set up a valid Service outside the lambda and place only the intended action inside it. A test of “no exception” can legitimately use assertDoesNotThrow when that is the complete promise, but it does not establish a return value or state change.

practice.title: Does this compile, and what does it check?
practice.prompt:
Contract: static int capAtTen(int n) returns n when n ≤ 10 and returns 10 otherwise. Negative integers are allowed. Assume the method is available in the test class and Jupiter imports are present.

@Test
void capsLargeNumber() {
    assertTrue(capAtTen(12));
}
practice.hint: Read the production return type before choosing the assertion.
practice.solution: assertEquals(10, capAtTen(12));

options.text: It does not compile: assertTrue requires a boolean expression.
options.feedback: capAtTen returns int, which Java does not treat as true or false.

options.text: It passes when the returned int is nonzero.
options.feedback: Java has no implicit int-to-boolean conversion here.

options.text: It checks that the returned int equals 10.
options.feedback: No equality comparison or expected value is present.

practice.title: What is wrong with these tests?
practice.prompt: Select the correct diagnoses.
practice.hint: Separate language rules, test-design choices and conventions.
practice.solution: The first, second and fourth statements are correct. JUnit does not require exactly one assertion.

options.text: assertEquals(actual, expected) may still compare correctly, but reverses failure-report labels.
options.feedback: Expected-first order is needed for trustworthy diagnostics.

options.text: A test that uses the implementation itself to calculate the expected value can repeat the same defect.
options.feedback: The expected result should come from the contract or another independent oracle.

options.text: Any test containing two assertions is invalid JUnit.
options.feedback: Several related assertions are valid; separate scenarios when that improves diagnosis.

options.text: A test that relies on another test having run first can be order-dependent.
options.feedback: Use fresh setup or an explicit single scenario, rather than hidden dependencies.

practice.title: Repair the expected value and its source
practice.prompt:
Contract: static int capAtTen(int n) returns n when n ≤ 10 and returns 10 otherwise. Negative integers are allowed. Assume the method is available in the test class and Jupiter imports are present.

@Test
void inputAboveTen() {
    int expected = capAtTen(13);
    assertEquals(expected, capAtTen(13));
}

Rewrite the test. Then describe a faulty implementation that the original would accept but your correction would reject.
practice.hint: A method that returns n unchanged produces identical wrong answers on both calls.
practice.solution:
@Test
void inputAboveTen_returnsTen() {
    assertEquals(10, capAtTen(13));
}

An implementation return n; makes the original compare 13 to 13. The repaired test compares the contract’s 10 with the incorrect 13 and fails.
rubric: Derives expected 10 from the contract.
Calls the intended method with a well-typed case.
Explains a concrete faulty implementation and the original false pass.

practice.title: Repair a test of the wrong exception source
practice.prompt:
new Counter(start) throws IllegalArgumentException for a negative start. void subtract(int amount) separately promises that a negative amount throws IllegalArgumentException. int get() reads the count; a rejected subtraction changes nothing.

@Test
void subtractNegative_throws() {
    assertThrows(IllegalArgumentException.class, () -> {
        Counter counter = new Counter(-1);
        counter.subtract(-3);
    });
}

Explain why this test can pass without exercising subtract. Rewrite it to isolate that operation and check the preserved state.

Assume org.junit.jupiter.api.Test and the static org.junit.jupiter.api.Assertions.* imports are present. Write the test methods inside a test class in the same package as the supplied API.
practice.hint: Create a valid counter outside the executable.
practice.solution:
@Test
void subtractNegative_preservesCount() {
    Counter counter = new Counter(5);
    assertThrows(IllegalArgumentException.class,
        () -> counter.subtract(-3));
    assertEquals(5, counter.get());
}

The original constructor throws first. The repaired constructor is valid and outside the lambda, so only the intended subtraction can satisfy the exception assertion.
rubric: Identifies the constructor as the original exception source.
Uses a valid initial count outside assertThrows.
Places only subtract(-3) inside the lambda.
Checks the documented unchanged count.

teachBack.prompt: What must you check before saying “the failed assertion proves a production bug”?
teachBack.answer: Confirm the setup, call and expected result agree with the current contract. Then inspect whether the observed difference can come from a test defect or unintended setup failure.

bridge: Next, turn verified evidence into a concise, reproducible defect report.

title: Write a defect report someone can reproduce
summary: Record the exact trigger, expectation and observation, then separate the symptom from the diagnosed cause.
goals: Write a defect record with a reproducible fixture and precise expected/actual result.
Read a stack trace as an execution location, not automatically a root cause.
Distinguish test messages, exception logging and a human-readable defect log.
setup: A useful report lets another person reproduce the failure and understand which promise it violates. “Does not work” leaves every decision to the reader. Start with the input and observation; state the root cause only when the code and trace support it.

worked.title: From a failed test to a clear error record
worked.intro:
Contract: Score.set(int) replaces the current score. new Score(3) starts at 3 and get() reads it. The production method currently uses score += value;.

@Test
void set_replacesExistingScore() {
    Score score = new Score(3);
    score.set(5);
    assertEquals(5, score.get(), "set must replace the old score");
}
ID: SCORE-01
Location: Score.set(int)
Contract: set(value) replaces the current score with value.
Reproduce: new Score(3); call set(5); observe get().
Expected: 5
Actual: 8
Detecting test: set_replacesExistingScore
Failure: expected <5> but was <8>
Cause: score += value adds the old score to the requested value.
Suggested correction: assign score = value.
Regression: keep this test; also test replacement with 0 and a negative int.
Status: reproduced; correction proposed, not yet verified.

steps.title: Make the fixture reproducible
steps.html: Both the initial 3 and replacement 5 matter. Without the starting state, someone could use zero and miss the defect. Record the class, method and operation sequence.

steps.title: Keep expected and actual separate
steps.html: Expected comes from “replaces.” Actual is the observed 8. Include the test name and assertion message so the evidence can be located quickly.

steps.title: Explain the causal operation
steps.html: The += uses the old field value, so 3 + 5 produces 8. This ties the implementation to the symptom. “Wrong answer” describes the symptom only.

steps.title: Describe verification honestly
steps.html: A suggested fix is not a verified fix. After applying it, rerun the reproducing test and relevant regression tests, then update the status with the observed outcome.

sections.title: Read a stack trace from the throw outward
sections.html:
java.lang.ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException: Index 2 out of bounds for length 2
    at Grid.get(Grid.java:18)
    at GridTest.lastCell_isReadable(GridTest.java:27)

The first frame identifies where this exception was thrown; the next shows the call from the test. It does not, by itself, establish why index 2 was reached. Check the test input and contract. If public indexes are one-based, a missing conversion may be the cause. If they are zero-based, the test might be invalid. Record actual line information from the current source, because line numbers can change.

sections.title: Three records with different jobs
sections.html:
RecordPurposeExample
JUnit failure messageExplain one violated expectation“set must replace the old score”
Defect log entryReproduce, diagnose and track a problemInput, expected/actual, test name, cause and verification status.
Application exception logRetain execution evidence for operation failuresOperation context, exception object and stack trace.

This fragment belongs inside a catch (java.io.IOException ex) block: ex is the caught exception. java.util.logging.Logger is Java’s logging class; getLogger returns a named logger object. Its three-argument log call takes a severity, a description, and the exception. Level.WARNING selects the severity.

java.util.logging.Logger logger =
    java.util.logging.Logger.getLogger("CountLoader");
logger.log(java.util.logging.Level.WARNING,
    "Could not load item counts", ex);

Passing the exception object retains stack/cause information; logging only ex.getMessage() loses it. Logging does not repair a failure or satisfy a test assertion. Choose one appropriate layer to report a propagated failure, avoid duplicating the same log at every layer, and avoid sensitive input in messages.

practice.title: Choose a reproducible report
practice.prompt: Contract: set(5) replaces the current score. Which report best supports investigation?
practice.hint: Could a second person reproduce the issue from the entry alone?
practice.solution: The first report supplies the minimum concrete evidence. Add a confirmed cause and proposed repair once inspected.

options.text: Score.set: starting at 3, set(5) leaves 8; expected 5. Test set_replacesExistingScore reproduces it.
options.feedback: It names the operation, fixture, expected result, actual result and detecting test.

options.text: The setter is broken sometimes.
options.feedback: There is no reproducible input or observed difference.

options.text: Change line 18. All tests fail.
options.feedback: A line suggestion without the violated contract or trigger does not explain the defect.

practice.title: What does the trace establish?
practice.prompt:
java.lang.NullPointerException
    at NameList.longest(NameList.java:42)
    at NameListTest.emptyList_hasNoLongest(NameListTest.java:18)

Select only what this trace directly establishes.
practice.hint: A trace records execution, not the complete specification.
practice.solution: It establishes the locations and call path. Root cause and responsibility require the contract, fixture and source.

options.text: The exception arose at the indicated location in NameList.longest.
options.feedback: The first frame identifies the throw location in this trace.

options.text: The indicated test called the operation along this stack.
options.feedback: The next frame shows the test’s call site.

options.text: The implementation must be wrong even if the test violates a precondition.
options.feedback: The contract and supplied fixture still need examination.

options.text: Changing every null to an empty String is the correct fix.
options.feedback: No such repair follows from the trace; it may violate the ADT contract.

practice.title: Write the defect entry
practice.prompt: Contract: int countPositive(int[] a) counts values strictly above zero; a is non-null. For {-1,0,2}, a test named zeroIsNotPositive expects 1 but observes 2. The method uses if (value >= 0) count++;. Write a compact report containing location, reproduction, expected/actual, test, cause, proposed fix and verification status.
practice.hint: State that the correction is proposed unless you actually have a rerun result.
practice.solution:
Location: countPositive(int[])
Reproduce: call countPositive(new int[]{-1, 0, 2}).
Expected: 1, because only 2 is strictly positive.
Actual: 2.
Test: zeroIsNotPositive; expected <1> but was <2>.
Cause: >= 0 incorrectly counts zero as positive.
Proposed fix: change the comparison to > 0.
Regression: retain the zero case and check empty/all-negative/all-positive arrays.
Status: reproduced; proposed fix not yet verified.
rubric: Contains the exact array and expected/actual values.
Names the method and test.
Links >= to including zero.
Gives a proposed correction and an honest status.

practice.title: Separate symptom and cause
practice.prompt: A linked collection’s remove operation disconnects a node but forgets to decrease its stored count. The observer int[] toArray() should contain exactly the stored values. It allocates using the stored count, then writes one element per reachable node. New int-array slots initially contain zero, so the oversized result exposes a trailing zero. A size test also reports the wrong number of stored values. Write one report explaining why these can be related symptoms. Then state the first regression test you would add.
practice.hint: Start at the operation that first breaks the invariant, rather than patching each observer.
practice.solution: The removal leaves the stored count larger than the reachable-node count. Allocation and traversal then disagree in toArray(); consumers inherit the inconsistent representation. Report removal as the confirmed cause when tracing verifies it, with each failing observer as supporting evidence. A first regression test removes the sole nonzero element, asserts size 0, and asserts an empty array. A second transition should remove one of two nodes and check the remaining value.
rubric: States count == reachable nodes as the broken invariant.
Distinguishes the original state defect from downstream observations.
Proposes a concrete removal-and-observation test.
Does not assume multiple failed tests always mean multiple root causes.

teachBack.prompt: Why should a report preserve the original failure even after a fix makes the test pass?
teachBack.answer: The original trigger and expected/actual values explain the defect and justify the regression test. Record the new verification result alongside that history rather than erasing the evidence.

bridge: Next, choose what to rerun and when a test expectation should legitimately change.

title: Fix the cause and keep the evidence
summary: Use regression tests to protect behavior, and revise expectations only when the contract changes.
goals: Use a red test, focused correction and regression checks as a debugging sequence.
Distinguish a defect fix from an intentional contract change.
Choose neighboring cases that could be affected by the correction.
setup: A regression test preserves evidence of a behavior that must keep working. A fix should make that test pass because the implementation meets the contract. Changing the expected value to whatever the current code returns removes the evidence instead of repairing the behavior.

worked.title: Fix an equality boundary, then check its neighbors
worked.intro:
// Contract: eligible ages are 18 and above.
static boolean eligible(int age) {
    return age > 18; // defect: excludes 18
}
@Test
void minimumAge_isEligible() {
    assertTrue(eligible(18));
}

Correction and neighboring tests:

static boolean eligible(int age) {
    return age >= 18;
}

@Test void belowMinimum_isIneligible() {
    assertFalse(eligible(17));
}
@Test void aboveMinimum_isEligible() {
    assertTrue(eligible(19));
}

steps.title: Reproduce before correcting
steps.html: The test for 18 fails against the original implementation. This shows it can detect this defect; a test that was never run against the defect gives less direct evidence.

steps.title: Change the operation responsible
steps.html: The contract includes equality. Changing > to >= includes exactly that boundary without changing the promise.

steps.title: Rerun the reproducer and related cases
steps.html: The 18 case should pass, while 17 stays false and 19 stays true. These neighbors help detect a repair that shifts the threshold or reverses the condition.

steps.title: Run the established regression suite
steps.html: Other callers may rely on the same helper. Run the relevant existing suite and investigate new failures. Record observed results; do not infer “all correct” from one green test.

sections.title: A new contract can require new tests
sections.html:
Suppose lookup(String key) previously returned null for an absent key. An explicit new contract now requires NoSuchElementException. The old absent-key test is no longer the right oracle. Update it, update documentation and implementation together, and keep tests for unchanged valid behavior.

// Old requirement:
assertNull(store.lookup("missing"));

// New requirement:
assertThrows(java.util.NoSuchElementException.class,
    () -> store.lookup("missing"));

This revision is justified by the changed requirement. A failing implementation alone is not a reason to change an expected result. Keep the key’s type and all unrelated setup valid.

sections.title: Rerun checks that answer a concrete question
sections.html:
• Reproducing test: did this exact defect disappear?
  • Boundary neighbors: did the correction shift or reverse a decision?
  • Other users of a helper: did shared behavior change?
  • State sequence: is an invariant still valid after later operations?
  • Established suite: did a previously covered behavior regress?

If a new failure appears, identify whether it reflects a wrong test, an intentional contract change, or an unintended behavior change. A large collection of green tests cannot decide those questions for you.

practice.title: Which change is a repair?
practice.prompt: Contract: eligible(18) must return true. The test expects true; the implementation returns false. Which response is justified by this information?
practice.hint: Which source establishes the expected behavior?
practice.solution: Keep the contract-based expectation and fix the implementation.

options.text: Correct the implementation and keep the boundary test.
options.feedback: The expected true follows the stated contract.

options.text: Change the test to expect false because that is the current output.
options.feedback: That encodes the defect as the new expectation.

options.text: Delete the test so the suite can pass.
options.feedback: Deleting the observation hides the defect.

practice.title: When should tests change?
practice.prompt: Select justified reasons to revise a test.
practice.hint: An expectation needs a reason independent of convenience.
practice.solution: A changed contract or a verified test defect justifies revising the test. Matching unexplained implementation output does not.

options.text: The documented contract intentionally changes from returning null to throwing a specific exception.
options.feedback: The oracle must track the approved requirement.

options.text: The test’s expected value is proven inconsistent with the unchanged contract.
options.feedback: Tests are code and can need correction.

options.text: The implementation fails the test, so any expectation matching its output is acceptable.
options.feedback: Failure alone does not show that the test is wrong.

options.text: The test’s constructor arguments do not compile against the supplied API.
options.feedback: The fixture must use the actual API before behavior can be tested.

practice.title: Choose a regression set
practice.prompt:
// Return true exactly when 0 <= n && n <= 5.
static boolean allowed(int n) {
    return n >= 0 && n < 5;
}

Give the correction and a compact boundary-focused set of input/expected pairs. Explain which case detects the original defect and which cases guard against overcorrection.
practice.hint: Use just outside, at and just inside the endpoints.
practice.solution:
Change n < 5 to n <= 5. A useful boundary set is:

nExpected
-1false
0true
1true
4true
5true
6false

The 5 case detects the original defect. The 6 case rejects an overly broad upper boundary; -1 and 0 preserve the lower boundary. Values 1 and 4 give nearby interior evidence.
rubric: Correctly includes both endpoints.
Includes the original witness n=5.
Includes values outside both ends with false expectations.
Explains why neighboring cases add distinct evidence.

practice.title: Update a changed exception contract
practice.prompt:
new ItemStore() creates an empty store. Previously Item find(String key) returned null for an absent key. Its new contract throws NoSuchElementException for an absent non-null key; null still throws NullPointerException. Write two independent Jupiter test methods for the new invalid cases, then name one existing kind of test that should remain.

Assume org.junit.jupiter.api.Test and the static org.junit.jupiter.api.Assertions.* imports are present. Write the test methods inside a test class in the same package as the supplied API.
practice.hint: Do not combine a null key with the absent-key case.
practice.solution:
@Test
void absentKey_throwsNoSuchElement() {
    ItemStore store = new ItemStore();
    assertThrows(java.util.NoSuchElementException.class,
        () -> store.find("absent"));
}

@Test
void nullKey_stillThrowsNullPointer() {
    ItemStore store = new ItemStore();
    assertThrows(NullPointerException.class, () -> store.find(null));
}

Keep successful lookup tests for existing keys, including the required returned item or identity if the contract specifies it.
rubric: Uses separate fresh fixtures.
Absent key is a real String, not null.
Each assertion expects the documented exception type.
Preserves normal lookup coverage.

teachBack.prompt: What does “all tests passed after my fix” establish, and what does it leave open?
teachBack.answer: The executed tests observed their specified expectations on those fixtures. It does not establish that the suite is complete, that every expected value is correct, or that untested paths meet the contract.

bridge: Next, build a complete suite from comments alone, without reading an implementation.

title: Design tests from comments alone
summary: Build a black-box test table, choose representatives, and translate the table into complete Jupiter tests.
goals: Extract types, normal behavior and invalid behavior from an unseen method’s contract.
Choose concrete representatives for each relevant class and boundary.
Write complete, well-typed tests with independent expected results.
setup: This lesson combines the whole workflow. Read the comment before selecting any assertion. A class of inputs such as “too long” is a design idea; an executable test also needs a concrete String and the expected result. Use the public promise to make both decisions.

worked.title: From one contract to a useful test table
worked.intro:
Only this public contract is available. Do not assume how the method is implemented.

/**
 * Returns true exactly when text has 2 through 8 characters inclusive
 * and every character is an ASCII letter A-Z or a-z.
 * Does not trim whitespace or modify the input.
 * Returns false for every other non-null String.
 * @throws NullPointerException if text is null
 */
public static boolean isValid(String text)

The method belongs to NameRules. The signature above is an API description; its implementation is intentionally hidden.

ReasonInputExpected
Null handlingnullNullPointerException
Below minimum"A"false
Minimum valid length"Ab"true
Interior valid length"Mira"true
Maximum valid length"Abcdefgh"true
Above maximum"Abcdefghi"false
Disallowed character at a valid length"A1"false
Whitespace is not trimmed" Ab"false
import org.junit.jupiter.api.Test;
import static org.junit.jupiter.api.Assertions.*;

class NameRulesTest {
    @Test
    void minimumLength_lettersAreAccepted() {
        assertTrue(NameRules.isValid("Ab"));
    }

    @Test
    void maximumPlusOne_isRejected() {
        assertFalse(NameRules.isValid("Abcdefghi"));
    }

    @Test
    void nullText_throws() {
        assertThrows(NullPointerException.class,
            () -> NameRules.isValid(null));
    }
}

steps.title: Read the signature
steps.html: The argument must be a String reference, and the method returns boolean. null is type-compatible but has a special documented response. A char such as 'A' is not a String argument.

steps.title: Separate independent requirements
steps.html:
Length and character membership are separate rules. To test the character rule, use a valid length; to test length, use only allowed letters. This keeps the reason for rejection clear.

The whitespace case uses " Ab": the contract rejects it, but incorrectly trimming first would turn it into the valid name "Ab". A space followed by only one letter would remain too short after trimming and would not expose that fault.

steps.title: Cover transitions, not just typical values
steps.html: The pairs 1/2 and 8/9 distinguish inclusive from exclusive endpoints. Null and empty are different cases. The empty String is also below minimum and can be added as its own structural case.

steps.title: Translate each observation
steps.html: Valid names use assertTrue; non-null rejected names use assertFalse; null uses assertThrows. The same general idea of “invalid” therefore needs different assertions.

sections.title: Explain why a case belongs
sections.html: A useful test comment records purpose, basis and assumptions. For example: “Black-box boundary test: eight allowed letters must be accepted because 8 is the documented inclusive maximum. Assumes the published contract applies; no implementation details are used.” The label black-box follows how you selected the case, not the assertion method you used.

sections.title: Do not invent promises
sections.html: The comment does not promise a particular exception message, speed or implementation strategy. Do not assert an invented message or demand a certain loop. It explicitly rejects spaces, so assuming automatic trimming would create a wrong test. For a missing rule, record the uncertainty rather than silently deciding the API’s behavior.

sections.title: Carry the same process to stored object values
sections.html: The final transfer task combines skills you already used: construct the required type, perform a void update, then inspect the state with a getter. For BigInteger, build arguments and expected values with BigInteger.valueOf(n) or BigInteger.ZERO. A replacement case needs an existing nonzero value so accidental addition is observable. A removal case needs an existing entry before the removal. The API’s objects change; the setup → action → observation pattern stays the same.

practice.title: Which are valid contract-based cases?
practice.prompt:
Only this public contract is available. Do not assume how the method is implemented.

/**
 * Returns true exactly when text has 2 through 8 characters inclusive
 * and every character is an ASCII letter A-Z or a-z.
 * Does not trim whitespace or modify the input.
 * Returns false for every other non-null String.
 * @throws NullPointerException if text is null
 */
public static boolean isValid(String text)

The method belongs to NameRules. The signature above is an API description; its implementation is intentionally hidden.

Select all correct input/expected pairs.
practice.hint: Use only the written promise, including the null exception.
practice.solution: The valid pairs are "Ab" → true, "A1" → false, and "" → false.

options.text: "Ab" → true
options.feedback: Two ASCII letters meet both requirements.

options.text: "A1" → false
options.feedback: Length is valid, but 1 is not an ASCII letter.

options.text: null → false
options.feedback: Null has the separate promised exception response.

options.text: " Ab " → true because names should be trimmed
options.feedback: The contract explicitly says no trimming; spaces are disallowed.

options.text: "" → false
options.feedback: An empty non-null String is below the minimum length.

practice.title: Isolate a character violation
practice.prompt:
Only this public contract is available. Do not assume how the method is implemented.

/**
 * Returns true exactly when text has 2 through 8 characters inclusive
 * and every character is an ASCII letter A-Z or a-z.
 * Does not trim whitespace or modify the input.
 * Returns false for every other non-null String.
 * @throws NullPointerException if text is null
 */
public static boolean isValid(String text)

The method belongs to NameRules. The signature above is an API description; its implementation is intentionally hidden.

Which rejected String best isolates the disallowed-character rule while satisfying the length rule?
practice.hint: Hold unrelated requirements valid.
practice.solution: Use "A1". A rejection then directly checks the character restriction.

options.feedback: It has a valid length of 2 and one non-letter.
It violates both the minimum length and the character rule.

options.text: "ABCDEFGHI1"
options.feedback: It violates both maximum length and the character rule.

practice.title: Write the missing boundary tests
practice.prompt:
Only this public contract is available. Do not assume how the method is implemented.

/**
 * Returns true exactly when text has 2 through 8 characters inclusive
 * and every character is an ASCII letter A-Z or a-z.
 * Does not trim whitespace or modify the input.
 * Returns false for every other non-null String.
 * @throws NullPointerException if text is null
 */
public static boolean isValid(String text)

The method belongs to NameRules. The signature above is an API description; its implementation is intentionally hidden.

Write two complete Jupiter test methods: one for eight letters and one for a single letter. Then add one sentence explaining why each case is useful. Assume imports are present.
practice.hint: Count the characters before choosing the expected boolean.
practice.solution:
@Test
void eightLetters_areAccepted() {
    assertTrue(NameRules.isValid("Abcdefgh"));
}

@Test
void oneLetter_isRejected() {
    assertFalse(NameRules.isValid("A"));
}

Eight letters test the inclusive upper endpoint. One letter tests the nearest value below the legal minimum. Both use allowed characters so only length varies.
rubric: Uses Strings of exactly 8 and 1 characters.
Uses @Test void methods and the correct static receiver.
Chooses assertTrue and assertFalse according to the contract.
Explains which boundaries the cases check.

practice.title: Transfer to object-valued counts
practice.prompt: Public API: CountMap() creates an empty map. void set(String key, BigInteger value) replaces a key’s count. Zero removes it; positive values store it; negatives throw IllegalArgumentException. Null key or value throws NullPointerException. BigInteger get(String key) returns the count, or BigInteger.ZERO when absent. Write a test that sets "pens" to 3 then 5 and checks 5, plus a separate test that removes an existing count by setting zero. Include the needed BigInteger import.
practice.hint: Both parameter and expected value need BigInteger objects; int literals alone are not BigInteger.
practice.solution:
import java.math.BigInteger;
import org.junit.jupiter.api.Test;
import static org.junit.jupiter.api.Assertions.*;

class CountMapTest {
    @Test
    void set_replacesExistingCount() {
        CountMap map = new CountMap();
        map.set("pens", BigInteger.valueOf(3));
        map.set("pens", BigInteger.valueOf(5));
        assertEquals(BigInteger.valueOf(5), map.get("pens"));
    }

    @Test
    void zero_removesExistingCount() {
        CountMap map = new CountMap();
        map.set("pens", BigInteger.valueOf(3));
        map.set("pens", BigInteger.ZERO);
        assertEquals(BigInteger.ZERO, map.get("pens"));
    }
}
rubric: Constructs BigInteger arguments instead of passing raw int values.
Uses a nonzero prior count to distinguish replacing from adding.
The zero case starts with an existing entry.
Expected values match the return type and precede actual values.

teachBack.prompt: Why does the word “invalid” not determine which JUnit assertion to use?
teachBack.answer: Different contracts reject inputs differently. A method may return false, return a sentinel, preserve state or throw a specific exception. Read the promised response for that input category.

bridge: Next, reveal an implementation and combine branch reasoning with defect and test review.

title: Review the implementation and its tests together
summary: Use a small trace to find a defect, repair a misleading test, and explain exactly what coverage does and does not show.
goals: Trace an implementation against its contract and choose a distinguishing witness.
Repair a weak test without changing the required behavior.
Connect branch evidence, a regression test and a defect report.
setup: You now have both a contract and an implementation. Use the contract for the expected result, and the code to understand which decisions the input exercises. These are complementary sources of evidence. A test can execute every branch and still miss a wrong boundary comparison.

worked.title: Full branch outcomes can still miss equality
worked.intro:
// Return the number of elements >= minimum.
// Empty arrays return 0. Null throws NullPointerException.
static int countAtLeast(int[] values, int minimum) {
    if (values == null) throw new NullPointerException("values");
    int count = 0;
    for (int i = 0; i < values.length; i++) {
        if (values[i] > minimum) { // defect
            count++;
        }
    }
    return count;
}
@Test
void valuesOnBothSides_areCounted() {
    assertEquals(1, countAtLeast(new int[]{2, 8}, 5));
}

This test sees both outcomes of the inner decision. It also enters and exits the loop and takes the non-null path. It does not test equality to 5.

@Test
void valueEqualToMinimum_isCounted() {
    assertEquals(1, countAtLeast(new int[]{5}, 5));
}

steps.title: Check the API first
steps.html: The inputs are int[] and int, and the result is int. new int[]{5} and 5 are valid arguments. Null is permitted as a Java reference value but must trigger the documented exception.

steps.title: Compare the promise to the decision
steps.html: “At least” includes equality. The code uses strict >, so an element equal to the minimum is not counted.

steps.title: Use the smallest distinguishing witness
steps.html: The single-element array {5} with minimum 5 should return 1. The loop runs once; the comparison is false; count stays 0. Changing the comparison to >= repairs this boundary.

steps.title: Keep the other cases
steps.html: Retain below/above values, empty input and null handling. The new equality test fills a behavioral gap; it does not make every other case redundant.

sections.title: Coverage needs a stated denominator
sections.html: For the shown code, if you count the null guard, loop condition and element comparison as three decisions with two outcomes each, the {2,8} case exercises five of the six outcomes: null=false, loop=true/false, comparison=true/false. A null case adds the sixth. Even then, equality can remain untested. Other tools may define or report branch counts differently; always state the decision set you are counting.

sections.title: A complete diagnosis has three parts
sections.html:
PartEvidence here
Contract violationAn equal element must be counted but is omitted.
Implementation explanationThe strict comparison is false on equality.
Test improvementAdd an equality case with an independent expected count.

A test that merely asserts the result is nonnegative would pass whether the answer is 0 or 1. Repairing the test and repairing production code are separate edits with separate reasons.

sections.title: Read another form of the same loop
sections.html:
The final task uses an enhanced for loop. for (int value : values) takes each int from the array in order and runs the body with that element assigned to value. It needs no explicit index or i++. An empty array runs the body zero times.

int[] values = new int[]{2, 5};
int total = 0;
for (int value : values) {
    total += value;
}

This fragment produces total 7. It visits the same elements as an indexed loop reading values[i]. A return inside its body still exits the entire method, just as in the earlier search example.

practice.title: Which case distinguishes > from >=?
practice.prompt:
// Return the number of elements >= minimum.
// Empty arrays return 0. Null throws NullPointerException.
static int countAtLeast(int[] values, int minimum) {
    if (values == null) throw new NullPointerException("values");
    int count = 0;
    for (int i = 0; i < values.length; i++) {
        if (values[i] > minimum) { // defect
            count++;
        }
    }
    return count;
}

Which input isolates the difference between the current comparison and the required comparison?
practice.hint: Find a value for which the two boolean expressions disagree.
practice.solution: Use an element exactly equal to the minimum, expecting it to count.

options.text: values = {5}, minimum = 5
options.feedback: Equality is false for > and true for >=.

options.text: values = {8}, minimum = 5
options.feedback: Both comparisons count 8.

options.text: values = {2}, minimum = 5
options.feedback: Both comparisons reject 2.

practice.title: Read the weak test
practice.prompt:
// Return the number of elements >= minimum.
// Empty arrays return 0. Null throws NullPointerException.
static int countAtLeast(int[] values, int minimum) {
    if (values == null) throw new NullPointerException("values");
    int count = 0;
    for (int i = 0; i < values.length; i++) {
        if (values[i] > minimum) { // defect
            count++;
        }
    }
    return count;
}
@Test
void countIsValid() {
    int actual = countAtLeast(new int[]{5}, 5);
    assertTrue(actual >= 0);
}

Which diagnoses are correct?
practice.hint: Separate syntax validity from how much behavior the assertion checks.
practice.solution: The first three statements are correct. The current condition is legal but insufficient for this expected count.

options.text: The test compiles: actual >= 0 is a boolean expression.
options.feedback: The integer comparison produces a boolean suitable for assertTrue.

options.text: The test passes for both the wrong 0 and the required 1.
options.feedback: Both results satisfy the weak condition.

options.text: Replacing the assertion with assertEquals(1, actual) checks the documented result.
options.feedback: The expected count follows the contract for this concrete input.

options.text: The only defect is using assertTrue; assertTrue is always bad for testing counts.
options.feedback: assertTrue is appropriate for a genuinely boolean property. Here the issue is the weak property selected.

practice.title: Write the focused regression and report
practice.prompt:
// Return the number of elements >= minimum.
// Empty arrays return 0. Null throws NullPointerException.
static int countAtLeast(int[] values, int minimum) {
    if (values == null) throw new NullPointerException("values");
    int count = 0;
    for (int i = 0; i < values.length; i++) {
        if (values[i] > minimum) { // defect
            count++;
        }
    }
    return count;
}

Write a complete Jupiter test for equality, then a compact defect explanation with input, expected, actual, cause and correction. Assume the static method is in IntStats and imports are present.
practice.hint: The implementation should supply the actual result; the comment supplies the expected 1.
practice.solution:
@Test
void equalElement_countsTowardMinimum() {
    assertEquals(1, IntStats.countAtLeast(new int[]{5}, 5));
}

Input {5}, minimum 5; expected 1, actual 0. The implementation uses strict >, excluding equality although “at least” includes it. Change the comparison to >=, then rerun this and the existing null, empty, below and above cases.
rubric: Uses the stated static class and well-typed arguments.
Tests equality with expected count 1.
Explains the actual 0 through the branch condition.
Names the correction and relevant regression cases.

practice.title: Transfer: early return inside a validator
practice.prompt:
Here for (int value : values) visits each array element in order; the body runs zero times for an empty array.

// Return true if every element is positive. Empty arrays return true.
// values must be non-null.
static boolean allPositive(int[] values) {
    for (int value : values) {
        if (value <= 0) return false;
        return true;
    }
    return true;
}

Choose a valid input revealing the defect, write the expected assertion, and describe the repair. Explain why a first element equal to zero does not expose this particular defect.
practice.hint: The first element must let execution reach the premature true return, while a later element violates the requirement.
practice.solution:
Use {2, 0}. The method wrongly returns true after inspecting 2, although 0 makes the required result false.

assertFalse(allPositive(new int[]{2, 0}));
