Remove the return true inside the loop. Keep the final true after all elements have been checked. A first zero already returns false correctly, so it does not expose the premature success path.
rubric: Chooses a positive first element and a later nonpositive element.
Uses assertFalse for the required result.
Moves success to the point where all elements have been checked.
Explains why a first-element rejection misses this defect.

teachBack.prompt: Why is branch coverage useful even though it does not guarantee correct results?
teachBack.answer: It exposes decisions that the suite never exercised. That helps choose additional cases. It does not verify the contract’s boundaries or the correctness of assertions, so combine it with contract-based expectations and distinguishing inputs.

title: Choose the method, write the test, explain the result
summary: Complete a mixed independent check: types, contracts, assertions, exceptions, state, production defects and defective tests.
goals: Choose a suitable testing approach without a chapter label giving it away.
Write compiling test methods with meaningful cases and correct assertions.
Explain defects and defend the expected behavior with evidence.
setup: Try the problems before opening hints or solutions. Work from a blank answer: identify the signature, extract the promise, choose a case, write the test, then explain what it detects. The written questions have checklists for comparison; they are not automatically compiled or graded. Run your Java in a real Jupiter project when checking compilation and execution.

worked.title: A short routine to use on any new method
worked.intro:
Use this checklist before answering the mixed practice. It is a decision routine, not a replacement for reading the supplied contract.

QuestionWhat to write down
What is available?Signature and comments only, or implementation too?
Will my call compile?Receiver, argument types/order/count, return type and imports.
What is promised?Return value, state change, exception and unchanged state.
Why this input?Partition, boundary, branch, state transition or concrete fault witness.
How will I observe it?The assertion and independent expected result.
What could fool this test?Weak oracle, invalid setup, aliasing, broad catch or wrong exception source.

steps.title: Design before writing syntax
steps.html: Write one input/expected pair in plain language. If you cannot state what should happen, pause at the contract instead of guessing an assertion.

steps.title: Translate into a test method
steps.html: Use @Test, a non-private void method, a valid fixture, the intended action and an assertion matching its result. Keep production return types separate from the test method’s return type.

steps.title: Challenge your own test
steps.html: Imagine one plausible faulty implementation. Would your test reject it? If it would still pass, decide whether the chosen property is too weak or whether another case is needed.

steps.title: Explain with evidence
steps.html: For a defect, provide input, expected, actual and the faulty operation. For an unclear requirement, identify what is unspecified. Do not convert uncertainty into an invented promise.

sections.title: How to review your written answers
sections.html: Use the solution as one valid answer, then check the criteria. Equivalent names and well-typed alternative assertions can be valid. A test may be logically sound but fail to compile, or compile while checking the wrong property; assess both. For explanations, insist on the causal link between the code and the observed behavior.

sections.title: What to do with a missed question
sections.html: If you chose an illegal argument, revisit types and signatures. If the expected result was wrong, revisit contracts and boundaries. If the assertion was wrong, revisit result types and Jupiter syntax. If you could not find a witness, revisit tracing and defect patterns. Then attempt a fresh case without the solution open. Reading a model answer and constructing one independently are different forms of practice.

practice.title: Problem 1: valid calls
practice.prompt: Available method: void setCount(String key, java.math.BigInteger count). Assume store is a valid receiver. No overloads exist. Select every call that is type-correct; this question does not ask whether the values satisfy the contract.
practice.hint: Decide Java type compatibility without inventing value restrictions.
practice.solution: The first, third and fifth calls compile against the signature. Passing compilation does not establish contract validity.

options.text: store.setCount("x", java.math.BigInteger.ONE);
options.feedback: String and BigInteger match the signature.

options.text: store.setCount("x", 1);
options.feedback: An int is not automatically converted to BigInteger.

options.text: store.setCount(null, null);
options.feedback: Both parameters have reference types. The contract may still reject these values.

options.text: store.setCount(1, "x");
options.feedback: Both argument types and their roles are wrong.

options.text: store.setCount("x", java.math.BigInteger.valueOf(-1));
options.feedback: The negative value is still a BigInteger; value validity is a separate question.

practice.title: Problem 2: read a contract
practice.prompt: int remove(String key) removes all matching entries and returns the number removed. For a null key it returns 0 and changes nothing. Which test checks the documented null behavior? Assume bag is a valid fixture.
practice.hint: Null does not universally mean an exception.
practice.solution: assertEquals(0, bag.remove(null)) checks the return promise. Add an observation of the contents when checking the unchanged-state promise.

options.text: assertEquals(0, bag.remove(null));
options.feedback: The method returns an int count; the contract promises zero for null.

options.text: assertThrows(NullPointerException.class, () -> bag.remove(null));
options.feedback: This invents a null rejection that the contract does not promise.

options.text: assertTrue(bag.remove(null));
options.feedback: The result is an int, not a boolean; this does not compile.

practice.title: Problem 3: construct the test
practice.prompt: RangeRules.allowed(int n) is a static method returning true exactly when 3 ≤ n ≤ 7. Write two complete Jupiter test methods: one for the inclusive upper endpoint, and one for the nearest integer above it. Include imports and a test class.
practice.hint: Use 7 and 8 and select assertions from their promised boolean outcomes.
practice.solution:
import org.junit.jupiter.api.Test;
import static org.junit.jupiter.api.Assertions.*;

class RangeRulesTest {
    @Test
    void upperEndpoint_isAllowed() {
        assertTrue(RangeRules.allowed(7));
    }

    @Test
    void aboveUpperEndpoint_isRejected() {
        assertFalse(RangeRules.allowed(8));
    }
}
rubric: Uses Jupiter imports consistently.
Uses @Test void methods inside a class.
Tests 7→true and 8→false with valid int calls.
Keeps each distinct scenario understandable.

practice.title: Problem 4: audit an exception test
practice.prompt:
new Balance(5) creates balance 5. withdraw(int amount) throws IllegalArgumentException for negative amounts and otherwise subtracts amount; there are no other restrictions in this example. Rejected calls leave the balance unchanged. int get() reads it.

@Test
void rejectsNegativeWithdrawal() {
    Balance balance = new Balance(5);
    try {
        balance.withdraw(-1);
    } catch (IllegalArgumentException ex) {
        assertEquals(5, balance.get());
    }
}

Explain a false-pass path, then rewrite using assertThrows and check the state.

Assume org.junit.jupiter.api.Test and the static org.junit.jupiter.api.Assertions.* imports are present. Write the test methods inside a test class in the same package as the supplied API.
practice.hint: What happens when withdraw wrongly accepts -1?
practice.solution:
If no exception is thrown, the catch is skipped and the method ends without an assertion. The test can pass even if the balance changes.

@Test
void negativeWithdrawal_preservesBalance() {
    Balance balance = new Balance(5);
    assertThrows(IllegalArgumentException.class,
        () -> balance.withdraw(-1));
    assertEquals(5, balance.get());
}
rubric: Explains the no-exception false pass.
Keeps valid setup outside the lambda.
Checks the required exception and unchanged state.

practice.title: Problem 5: diagnose the implementation
practice.prompt:
// Return the sum of all elements. values is non-null.
static int sum(int[] values) {
    int total = 0;
    for (int i = 1; i < values.length; i++) {
        total += values[i];
    }
    return total;
}

Give a small valid witness, expected versus actual, one regression assertion and the correction. Then explain why testing only an empty array would miss this defect.
practice.hint: The loop starts at index 1.
practice.solution:
Use {7}. Expected sum is 7; actual is 0 because the loop never visits index 0. Start the loop at 0.

assertEquals(7, sum(new int[]{7}));

The empty array has the correct sum 0 even in the faulty code, so it does not reveal the skipped first element.
rubric: Uses a valid array containing a nonzero first element.
Traces the skipped index 0.
States independent expected and actual values.
Uses expected-first assertEquals and corrects the initializer.

practice.title: Problem 6: observe an ADT transition
practice.prompt:
new StringStack() creates an empty stack. void push(String) adds a non-null value. String pop() removes and returns the newest value; empty pop throws NoSuchElementException. int size() returns the count. Write a test that pushes "a" then "b", removes both in the correct order, checks size zero and checks one further pop.

Assume org.junit.jupiter.api.Test and the static org.junit.jupiter.api.Assertions.* imports are present. Write the test methods inside a test class in the same package as the supplied API.
practice.hint: The stack is last-in, first-out. The final pop is an exception observation.
practice.solution:
@Test
void stack_returnsNewestFirst_thenRejectsEmptyPop() {
    StringStack stack = new StringStack();
    stack.push("a");
    stack.push("b");
    assertEquals("b", stack.pop());
    assertEquals("a", stack.pop());
    assertEquals(0, stack.size());
    assertThrows(java.util.NoSuchElementException.class, () -> stack.pop());
}
rubric: Uses LIFO order b then a.
Checks count after removals.
Places the empty pop inside assertThrows.
Uses String and int expectations for their corresponding results.

practice.title: Problem 7: interpret coverage and evidence
practice.prompt: A suite exercises true and false for every counted decision in a method, and every test passes. Select the conclusions supported by that information.
practice.hint: Coverage describes execution; assertions compare selected observations.
practice.solution: The first, third and fifth statements are supported. Keep contract-based boundaries and test review alongside coverage evidence.

options.text: Both outcomes of each decision in the stated coverage model were exercised.
options.feedback: That is what the supplied coverage statement establishes.

options.text: Every input and every possible path has been tested.
options.feedback: Branch outcomes do not enumerate all values or path combinations.

options.text: The executed assertions accepted the observed results in those runs.
options.feedback: That is the direct meaning of passing test executions.

options.text: The expected results and test setup must all be correct.
options.feedback: A test can have a wrong or weak oracle and still pass.

options.text: An equality-boundary defect may still remain.
options.feedback: Tests on either side can cover both outcomes without testing equality.

practice.title: Problem 8: write the error record
practice.prompt: Contract: int boundedCount(int n) returns 0 for negative n and returns n otherwise. Test zeroRemainsZero passes. Test negativeBecomesZero calls boundedCount(-2), expects 0 and observes -2. Implementation: return n;. Write a clear defect report and propose two further tests with expected results. Explain why the passing zero case did not establish correctness.
practice.hint: Use the report structure from lesson 26 and cover a different negative value plus a normal positive one.
practice.solution:
Location: boundedCount(int)
Contract: negative inputs become 0; other inputs are unchanged.
Reproduce: boundedCount(-2).
Expected: 0.
Actual: -2.
Test: negativeBecomesZero.
Cause: return n performs no negative-value check.
Proposed fix: if (n < 0) return 0; otherwise return n.
Regression: -1 -> 0; 4 -> 4; retain 0 -> 0 and -2 -> 0.
Status: reproduced; proposed fix not yet verified.

The faulty implementation happens to return the correct value for zero. One passing case did not exercise the negative-input behavior.
rubric: Provides method, exact trigger, expected/actual and test name.
Connects the unchanged negative value to the missing condition.
Suggests a contract-preserving repair and nonredundant tests.
Does not claim the unrun repair was verified.

teachBack.prompt: Can you justify the input, expected result and assertion in every test you wrote, without opening its solution?
teachBack.answer: Use that question to identify the next practice target. If the input is sound but syntax is uncertain, practise construction. If syntax is sound but the case is weak, practise test selection. Repeat a fresh mixed set after revisiting the specific gap.
